bullets: Stave 1: the charity collectors call at the counting-house on Christmas Eve to collect money for the poor.
Stave 4: the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come takes Scrooge to a squalid corner of the city where his belongings are sold.
Stave 5: Scrooge meets the gentleman in the street and makes a generous donation.
These characters are unnamed (except Mrs Dilber and Old Joe) and function as types: charity, theft, greed.
They also show Dickens’s skill at brief, vivid characterisation using speech and a few physical details.
core.h: Overview: three small groups with large functions
core.p: Minor characters in A Christmas Carol are rarely just background. The two gentlemen who ask for charity in Stave 1 prompt Scrooge’s most notorious statements; the same gentleman returns in Stave 5 to show how far he has changed. Mrs Dilber, the other women and the undertaker’s man in Stave 4 appear as ordinary people exploiting Scrooge’s death, and Old Joe is the dealer who buys the stolen goods. Each group lets Dickens show something about Scrooge from outside, through the eyes of the community.

rows: Ask Scrooge to give; he refuses, later reverses
Scrooge’s ideology; Dickens’s attack on the Poor Law; measure of change
Sell Scrooge’s belongings after his death
Consequence of isolation; “every man for himself” turned on Scrooge
Moral squalor; market that prices everything

bullets: The collector’s appeal: “Many thousands are in want of common necessaries” and hundreds of thousands lack comforts; they choose this season because Want is “keenly felt” and Abundance rejoices.

Scrooge’s answers are quick, hostile and legalistic. He asks “Are there no prisons?” and is told there are “plenty”; he then asks whether the Union workhouses are still in operation, and the Treadmill and the Poor Law are named as in full vigour.
He is told that “many would rather die” than enter a workhouse, and replies that they had better do it and “decrease the surplus population”: Malthusian cruelty in plain words.
He says that it is not his business to interfere with other people’s: self-interest as a creed; his own occupation “occupies me constantly”.
The exchange ends abruptly with “Good afternoon, gentlemen!”, a polite phrase used as a weapon.
The scene also introduces the Poor Law and Treadmill: Dickens uses a short dialogue to embed a whole social argument.

callouts.p: Scrooge is allowed to condemn himself in his own words. The reader hears an economic argument made without pity, and the contrast with the collector’s gentle plea makes the argument seem cruel.

Link the exchange to the Poor Law of 1834 and to Malthus’s ideas of surplus population, but only as part of an analytical point, for example that Scrooge repeats government policy without thinking about the people it harms.

core.p: The collectors enter with formal politeness and ask for money to buy “meat and drink” and “means of warmth” for the poor. Dickens makes them reasonable, middle-class, and courteous: they refer to Marley’s “liberality”, which they assume is “well represented by his surviving partner”. This is ironic, because Scrooge is anything but liberal. By making them polite, Dickens allows the reader to hear Scrooge’s harshness all the more clearly.

bullets: The gentleman’s astonishment is a way to show the reader how complete the change is; the community needs to see it too.
“back-payments” is an economic term: Scrooge frames his generosity as repayment of a debt to the poor, linking money to moral duty.
The gentleman’s cautious politeness and shaking hands show relief; he is not triumphant but moved.
Scrooge’s reform is practical: he gives money, not only feelings. Dickens implies that real charity must be active.
The scene is short and brisk; it does not sentimentalise, and moves quickly on to church and to Fred’s house.

callouts.p: In a part (b) answer on change, compare the two collector scenes: the same characters, the same request, opposite responses. Name this as ring composition or a cyclical structure.

core.h: The charity collector returns in Stave 5
core.p: In Stave 5, Scrooge sees one of the gentlemen in the street and approaches him with courtesy and humility. He asks forgiveness (“allow me to ask your pardon”), and when he names the sum, “not a farthing less”, adding that “a great many back-payments are included”, the gentleman is so shocked that he exclaims “Lord bless me!” as if his breath were gone. This creates a cyclical structure: the first meeting shows Scrooge’s hardness and the second shows his reform in the same setting.

bullets: Setting: a “low-browed” shop at the edge of society; dirt, waste and smoke; Dickens’s Gothic realism.

The scavengers are casual and unashamed: “Every person has a right to take care of themselves”, with the bitter addition “He always did!” Their defence is Scrooge’s own philosophy of self-interest repeated.

One of them asks, in disgust at his meanness, why he was not “natural in his lifetime”: if he had been, he would have had somebody to look after him in his last hours. This ties the theft directly to his isolation.
Mrs Dilber is the laundress whose name Dickens gives, making her individual, and her complicity shows even the humblest people in his orbit felt no loyalty to him.
Old Joe is the market itself, the man who prices everything: “We’re all suitable to our calling, we’re well matched.” His moral fluency makes him chilling.
The items are intimate (bed-curtains, blankets, a shirt); Scrooge is being stripped literally and symbolically.
Scrooge’s reaction is disgust at them as “demons, marketing the corpse itself”: he cannot see that he created the conditions in which people value goods above him.

callouts.p: The charwoman, the laundress (Mrs Dilber) and the undertaker’s man all appear in this scene. In an exam, refer to them as “the scavengers” unless you are certain which speaker said which line in your own copy.

core.h: Mrs Dilber, the other scavengers and Old Joe (Stave 4)
core.p: In Stave 4, the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come leads Scrooge to a squalid, narrow part of the town. In a “beetling shop” that deals in rags, bones and scraps, a group of two women and an undertaker’s man arrive to sell items they have taken from the dead man’s room, which Scrooge does not at first recognise as his own. Old Joe, a “grey-haired rascal”, pays them small sums. Their talk is light, brisk and mocking, and they laugh as if sharing a joke, which makes the scene more chilling.

head: Detail
Quotation or image
Effect
rows: Moral and physical squalor; Scrooge’s wealth ends here
“Every person has a right to take care of themselves”
The most personal items are traded

bullets: Colloquial dialect and contractions make the scavengers sound real and ordinary, not villainous: “’em”, “lifetime”.
Sibilance and harsh consonants in the description of the shop (rags, bones, greasy offal) create a sensory disgust.
The repeated laughter is a motif that shows indifference; it also contrasts with the warm laughter of Fred’s party.
Scrooge is a witness and the Ghost is silent; there is no authorial comment; the reader must draw the moral.
Setting is a character: the shop is below ground level, hidden and dirty, like a metaphor for the moral underworld.
Juxtaposition: the businessmen on the Exchange (indifferent) and the thieves (greedy) show different forms of lack of mourning.

callouts.p: The people stealing from Scrooge reflect the values he held. Their callous self-interest is his own creed applied to him, which is the Ghost’s lesson and Dickens’s warning: a society that denies community creates people who will rob the dead.

core.h: Language and structure in the Stave 4 scene
core.p: Dickens deliberately uses short, quick exchanges to give a feeling of overheard, dirty gossip. The scene is also structured as a sequence of items: the women unwrap the bundles, Old Joe prices each, and Scrooge watches. This catalogue structure is a kind of auction and emphasises that Scrooge’s life is reduced to objects. The humour is dark, because the speakers laugh as they strip a dead man.

callouts.p: Do not say the Poor Law existed. Say that Scrooge’s question about workhouses reflects the harsh official view that poverty was a moral failing, which Dickens exposes as callous.

core.p: For these characters, the best context is the Victorian approach to poverty and charity, the Poor Law and the economic ideas that justified it, and the reality of cities where poor people scavenged for a living. Dickens drew on his observation of London and on reports about poverty.

bullets: Moral reading: the scavengers are greedy, and their lack of respect for the dead reflects a society that has lost its moral compass.
Social reading: they are poor people surviving in a system that gives them nothing, so their behaviour is a result of poverty, not just greed.
Ironic reading: they are exact mirrors of Scrooge: the wealthy man’s principle is practised by the poor.
Collector reading: Dickens uses them to show the weakness of polite charity against political and economic power; real change requires Scrooge himself to change.
Humour reading: the dark comedy of the thieves lets Dickens criticise through satire, not only horror.

callouts.p: The minor characters give the community’s view of Scrooge: pitying, mocking or indifferent. The novella’s purpose is to make him want to be remembered differently.

core.p: Different readers can find different emphases in these minor characters. Some see the collectors as Dickens’s own voice, a decent middle-class perspective on poverty, while others see them as passive: the collectors have no answer for Scrooge. The scavengers may be villains, victims or products of Scrooge’s own economic world.

callouts.p: Do not invent details about Mrs Dilber. Dickens gives very little, and a short precise use of her complicity is better than a long guess.

core.p: These characters are valuable because they give you short, memorable, quotable lines that you can analyse closely. They also help you answer questions on poverty, charity, community, redemption, Scrooge’s change and Dickens’s social criticism. Use them as evidence for an argument about how Dickens uses other people to measure Scrooge.

The scavengers in Stave 4: mirrored creed, isolation, the market of Old Joe
The collector in Stave 5: cyclical structure and practical change
Evaluate purpose: character as a means to a social argument
essays.q: How does Dickens use minor characters to show Scrooge’s attitudes and his change? Refer to the charity collectors and one other minor character or group.
essays.text:
Dickens’s minor characters rarely have names, but they have a clear job: they let the reader see Scrooge from outside. Through the charity collectors and the scavengers of Stave 4, Dickens builds a moral argument that the novella’s hero must confront his own philosophy before he can change.

In Stave 1, the collectors are given a polite, almost scripted language. They speak of “many thousands” in want, and of hundreds of thousands who lack comforts, and the escalation turns poverty from a personal misfortune into a social fact. By making the collectors courteous and reasonable, Dickens makes Scrooge’s answers more shocking, because they arrive in the register of administration: “Are there no prisons?” and “Are there no workhouses?” are rhetorical questions that treat institutions as an answer to human need. His claim that the poor might “decrease the surplus population” draws on Malthusian language that was influential in the 1834 Poor Law debates, and Dickens’s decision to give it to Scrooge is itself satirical, since it implies that the policy is the speech of a miser.

In Stave 4, the minor characters change from victims of Scrooge’s policy to its imitators. Old Joe’s “beetling shop” is described with sensory disgust, and the grey-haired rascal is a figure of comic menace: his familiarity with theft makes the scene chilling. The scavengers laugh, and one defends herself with the words “Every person has a right to take care of themselves”, adding “He always did!” The line is the most pointed irony of the novella. The philosophy Scrooge used to refuse the collectors is now applied to his own bed-curtains. Dickens suggests that a world which teaches people to mind only their own business will teach them to rob the dead. At the same time, the scavengers are poor, and their behaviour could also be read as survival, which complicates the moral judgement and shows Dickens’s sympathy.

Scrooge’s own reaction, a disgust that sees “demons, marketing the corpse itself”, is also an ironic failure of recognition. The verb “marketing” is commercial, and so the horror is that the dead man has become a product, as he treated living people. The Ghost is silent, which means the reader must make the connection.

The novella then closes the loop. In Stave 5, Scrooge meets the collector in the street and gives “not a farthing less” than a large sum, adding that “a great many back-payments” are included. The financial vocabulary survives, but its moral content is reversed: money is now repayment to the community rather than a barrier against it. The gentleman’s amazement is also the reader’s evidence that the change is real. The cyclical structure, with the same request and a new answer, shows that Dickens’s purpose is not only to condemn but to demonstrate that the habits of a lifetime can be undone.
essays.thesis: Dickens uses minor characters as moral mirrors: the collectors expose Scrooge’s creed and later measure his reform, while the scavengers of Stave 4 show that a society built on self-interest turns even the dead into goods.

quotes.a: The collector’s polite but statistical language sets the scale of the problem. “Many thousands” and the escalation to “hundreds of thousands” turn poverty into a social fact, not a personal failing. The formal, balanced sentence structure shows the collector as reasonable, which makes Scrooge’s reply seem harsher.
quotes.q: Many thousands are in want of common necessaries

quotes.a: The phrase is a polite compliment that is bitterly ironic: the reader already knows Scrooge’s character. It shows the collector’s assumption that wealthy men are generous, which is an assumption Scrooge shatters. It also reminds readers of Marley, whose ghost is coming.
quotes.c: Expectation that rich businessmen subscribed to charity.
quotes.q: well represented by his surviving partner

quotes.a: The gentleman’s reply is dry and weary: there are plenty of prisons, so society has chosen punishment over relief. His tone suggests he repeats the official answer without agreeing with it, so Dickens’s criticism of Poor Law policy comes from a decent, moderate man rather than a radical, which makes it harder for readers to dismiss.
quotes.c: The Poor Law and the link between poverty and punishment.

quotes.a: The verb “decrease” and the abstract “surplus population” are cold, administrative language that turns people into numbers. Dickens uses Malthusian terms to show Scrooge’s moral blindness; the line returns in Stave 3 when the Ghost quotes it about Tiny Tim, which transforms it into an indictment.
quotes.c: Malthus and the economic debate around population.

quotes.a: The exclamation is polite on the surface but is used to end the conversation as a door slammed shut. The contrast between courtesy and cruelty shows how Scrooge uses social forms as weapons, and the exclamation mark shows impatience. The tone is also dismissive, as if the collectors were servants.
quotes.c: Victorian politeness as a mask for class power.

quotes.a: A farthing is the smallest coin, so the phrase means every penny; Scrooge insists on giving the full amount, with no discount, reversing his previous miserliness. The financial vocabulary is deliberate: his generosity is expressed in the language that once defined his meanness.

The compound noun frames his gift as a repayment of a debt that has accumulated over years of neglect. It suggests that the rich owe something to the poor, not the other way round. The business word is a sign of how Scrooge’s moral vocabulary has changed while keeping his accountant’s habits.

The speaker defends theft as self-preservation; it is a direct echo of Scrooge’s own ideology that each person minds their own business. The addition “He always did!” turns the line into a cruel joke at his expense. The irony is that the poor learn selfishness from the rich.
quotes.q: Every person has a right to take care of themselves

quotes.a: A “screw” is slang for a miser, and “wicked” is an unusually moral judgement from a thief. The collocation shows that even those on the edge of morality condemn Scrooge, and the colloquial tone turns the condemnation into everyday gossip. It tells the reader how the community remembers him.

“Beetling” suggests an overhanging, brooding structure, and also the creeping of insects; it gives the shop a sinister, animal feeling. The shop is both literally low and morally low. The setting prepares the reader for a scene of moral decay.

The word “rascal” is playful, almost affectionate, which makes Old Joe more disturbing, because he is a criminal who is treated as a character in a comic tale. “Grey-haired” suggests age and experience, so his dishonesty is a lifelong habit. Dickens’s humour is a trap for the reader’s sympathy.

The simile compares the scavengers to demons and names their activity with a commercial verb, “marketing”. The effect is of religious horror and economic satire combined: they turn a human body into goods. Scrooge’s disgust is also a failure to recognise himself, since he too turned people into profit.
quotes.c: Victorian anxieties about the commercialisation of death.

summary: The two charity collectors (Stave 1 and Stave 5), Mrs Dilber and her fellow scavengers, and Old Joe (Stave 4) are minor characters who expose Scrooge’s ideology, show the effect of his isolation, and measure his change.
